notes.meaning: Moses tells the people to love the LORD and always keep His charges, rules, and commands. Real obedience is never just empty routine; it must grow out of genuine love for God. Loving the Lord is an active choice His people are called to make every day.

Moses reminds the people that he is not addressing their young children, who never witnessed God's mighty acts. Instead, he speaks to the older generation who experienced God's discipline, majesty, and power firsthand. Remembering how God has corrected and guided us in the past helps us trust Him today.

Moses reminds them of the great signs and wonders God performed in Egypt against Pharaoh and his entire country. He also recounts how God swept the Egyptian army, horses, and chariots into the Red Sea when they gave chase. That dramatic rescue destroyed Egypt's military might so completely that its effects lasted for generations.

Moses recalls how the LORD faithfully cared for Israel throughout forty years in the desert, while also disciplining the nation when it rebelled. When Dathan and Abiram led a revolt against Moses' God-given authority, the earth split open and swallowed them, their families, and their tents. God stopped that dangerous rebellion immediately to save the wider nation from ruining itself.

The people listening to Moses were personal eyewitnesses to all the great things God had done. Because they had seen these wonders with their own eyes, they could not claim they did not know God's power. Seeing God work in our lives gives us a special duty to stay loyal to Him.

Moses urges the people to keep all of God's commands so they will have the strength to cross the Jordan and take the land. Faithfulness to God would give them courage in battle and victory over their enemies. Obedience was also the key to living long and thriving in a rich country flowing with milk and honey.

Moses explains that the Promised Land is very different from Egypt, where farmers had to work hard to channel water from the Nile with their feet. Canaan is a land of hills and valleys that depends entirely on rain falling from the sky. It is a special place that the LORD watches over constantly, caring for it from the start of the year to the end.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that portraying Canaan as watered by rain rather than human irrigation was meant to highlight Israel's direct dependence on God.

notes.meaning: God promises that if His people truly love Him and serve Him with their whole heart, He will send rain right on schedule. The autumn rains would help the newly planted seeds sprout, while the spring rains would swell the grain, grapes, and olives for harvest. He would also provide lush pasture for their animals so everyone had plenty to eat.

Moses warns the people not to let their hearts be tricked into bowing down to false gods once life becomes comfortable. If they turn away from the LORD, His anger will burn against them, and He will close the skies so no rain falls. Without crops and water, they would quickly perish from the fertile land God gave them.

The Israelites were told to store God's words deep inside their hearts and minds. They were also commanded to bind them on their hands and foreheads as constant reminders of His truth. Keeping God's Word front and center in our thoughts helps direct everything we do.

Parents were charged to teach God's words to their children throughout the normal rhythms of daily life. They were to speak of them when sitting at home, walking down the road, going to sleep, and getting up in the morning. Writing them on doorposts and gates kept God's truth visible to the whole family and community.

Faithfully keeping and passing on God's law would allow the people and their children to enjoy long lives in the promised land. Their time there would be as secure and enduring as the heavens above the earth. A nation's lasting peace depends on honoring God from generation to generation.

Moses promises that if Israel carefully obeys God's commands, loves Him, and clings to Him, the LORD will drive out all the nations before them. Even though the Canaanite peoples were bigger and more powerful, God would give Israel the victory. True spiritual success comes not from our own strength, but from walking closely with God.

God promises that every piece of ground the Israelites step on within the promised borders will belong to them. Their territory would stretch from the southern wilderness up to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates River west to the Mediterranean Sea. The LORD would cause all the surrounding peoples to fear them, so no enemy could successfully stand in their way.

Moses places a clear choice before the people: a blessing or a curse. They would receive God's blessing if they obeyed His commandments, but they would fall under a curse if they chased after idols they had never known. God makes our moral choices matter, urging us to choose the way of obedience and life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that framing the choice as blessings and curses follows the standard pattern of ancient Near Eastern treaties.

notes.meaning: Once Israel crossed into the land, they were to proclaim God's blessings from Mount Gerizim and His curses from Mount Ebal. These two peaks stood opposite one another near Shechem, close to the oak trees where God had first appeared to Abraham. Announcing the covenant, which was God's solemn agreement with them, in that historic place would remind them of His long-standing faithfulness.

Israel was about to cross the Jordan River to conquer and settle the land God was giving them. Moses reminds them that taking possession of the land brought a solemn responsibility to obey all of God's rules and laws. Receiving God's gifts should always lead to thankful, obedient living.
